claims.claim: Where signal correlations are positive, positive noise correlations should reduce discriminability by increasing the overlap between neural responses evoked by discriminanda.
claims.source: Under these conditions, where signal correlations are positive, positive noise correlations should reduce discriminability (Averbeck et al., 2006) by increasing the overlap between neural responses evoked by discriminanda.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on theoretical work cited and logical inference.

claims.claim: Sessions in which low-frequency laser-induced correlations caused the strongest perceptual suppression all showed negative NDMIs.
claims.source: In both analyses, the sessions in which low-frequency laser-induced correlations caused the strongest perceptual suppression all showed negative NDMIs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the relationship between NDMI and PDMI shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Laser-induced reductions in discriminability at the neural level corresponded to increased perceptual thresholds.
claims.source: In other words, laser-induced reductions in discriminability at the neural level corresponded to increased perceptual thresholds.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the correlation between NDMI and PDMI shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There was no significant correlation between NDMI and changes in the slope of the psychometric function.
claims.source: There was no significant correlation between NDMI and changes in the slope of the psychometric function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between NDMI and slope changes.

claims.claim: NDMI calculated from hit trials had no correlation with threshold or slope changes.
claims.source: NDMI calculated from hit trials had no correlation with threshold or slope changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of NDMI from hit trials.

claims.claim: It is possible to induce coherent activity in a neuronal ensemble due to sub-threshold rhythmic stimulation.
claims.source: To confirm whether it is possible to induce coherent activity in a neuronal ensemble due to sub-threshold rhythmic stimulation, we examined the consequences of such stimulation on a conductance-based model of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Figure 6A; see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Sub-threshold stimulation can induce coherent activity in the network at a desired frequency.
claims.source: We find that it is indeed possible to induce coherent activity in the network at a desired frequency (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and that this induction is robust to a wide range of network (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) and stimulation parameters (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6D and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The location specificity of the impairment suggests that the impairment is not due to a phosphene effect.
claims.source: The location specificity of the impairment also suggests that the impairment is not due to a phosphene effect (Jazayeri et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial specificity of the behavioral effect and citation to prior work on phosphenes.

claims.claim: If attention were drawn away from the unstimulated location by a phosphene, impaired performance would be expected in the attend-away condition.
claims.source: If attention were drawn away from the unstimulated location by a phosphene we would expect impaired performance in the attend-away condition.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if a phosphene were causing the effect.

claims.claim: Stimulation at a non-opsin site does not cause changes in behavior.
claims.source: We also verified that the impairment was not due to a thermal effect by stimulating a location in the chamber a few millimeters from the opsin site (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and not due to visual distractions caused by the laser light by stimulating outside the brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B). In both cases, we did not observe any changes in behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Stimulation outside the brain does not cause changes in behavior.
claims.source: We also verified that the impairment was not due to a thermal effect by stimulating a location in the chamber a few millimeters from the opsin site (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) and not due to visual distractions caused by the laser light by stimulating outside the brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B). In both cases, we did not observe any changes in behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: It is reasonable to assume that the opsin was strongly biased toward pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: Thus, we do not have a measure of lenti/CAMKII selectivity in macaque V4. However, it is reasonable to assume that the opsin was strongly biased toward pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior work showing selectivity in V1 and other brain areas.

claims.claim: In a previous study in V1, lenti/CAMKII expressing C1V1/EYFP led to expression that was highly selective for excitatory neurons.
claims.source: In that study, lenti/CAMKII expressing C1V1/EYFP led to expression that was highly selective for excitatory neurons (Figure 1B of Nassi et al., 2015): of 119 neurons imaged in five different fields of view, only 2 (1.7%) were double labeled for both EYFP and parvalbumin/calretinin/calbindin, indicating that expression was heavily biased toward excitatory neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: CaMKII has been used in other macaque brain areas including perirhinal cortex, where it led to opsin expression primarily in excitatory neurons.
claims.source: CaMKII has also been used in other macaque brain areas including perirhinal cortex (Tamura et al., 2017), where it also led to opsin expression primarily in excitatory neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The results establish the first causal link between correlated variability and perception.
claims.source: Our results establish the first causal link between correlated variability and perception.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The optogenetic stimulation protocol induces correlations that might not be physiologically realistic.
claims.source: The optogenetic stimulation protocol in our study, using sinusoidal modulation of laser irradiance, induces the kind of correlations in a local population of the cortex that might not be physiologically realistic.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the experimental approach.

claims.claim: The study establishes the causal relevance of low-frequency correlated variability in perception.
claims.source: It nevertheless establishes the causal relevance of low-frequency correlated variability in perception and supports the hypothesis that attention-dependent reductions in correlated variability enhance perception.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The correlations induced in the study included information-limiting correlations.
claims.source: Recently, studies have theorized that only certain correlations – those that are indistinguishable from stimulus-induced correlations – are information limiting (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014). We speculate that the correlations induced in our study included such information-limiting correlations, resulting in the observed impairment.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on theoretical work and the observed results.

claims.claim: The timescale of low-frequency correlations is consistent with inter-saccadic intervals (200–300 ms).
claims.source: The timescale of these low-frequency correlations is consistent with inter-saccadic intervals (200–300 ms), which may be a relevant timeframe for gathering visual information (Yarbus et al., 1967).
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the timescale of correlations to a known behavioral timescale, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Decreases in correlated variability at the inter-saccadic timescale could be critical for perception.
claims.source: Decreases in correlated variability at this timescale could therefore be critical for perception.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the connection between correlation timescales and behavioral timescales.

claims.claim: Human observers are better able to discriminate stimulus orientations near the cardinal than oblique orientations.
claims.source: Psychophysical studies have found that human observers are better able to discriminate stimulus orientations near the cardinal than oblique orientations (Girshick et al., 2011; Heeley and Timney, 1988; Appelle, 1972; Orban et al., 1984; Campbell et al., 1966).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior psychophysical research.

claims.claim: Cardinal orientations are overrepresented in V1.
claims.source: Electrophysiological and imaging studies in humans, monkeys, cats and ferrets have found that cardinal orientations are overrepresented in V1 (De Valois et al., 1982; Furmanski and Engel, 2000; Li et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003; Chapman and Bonhoeffer, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological and imaging studies.

results.result: Low-frequency (4-5 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of V4 neurons impairs orientation discrimination performance in a spatially-specific manner. The impairment is observed only when attention is directed to the stimulated location (attend-in condition), with significant increases in perceptual thresholds across 42 behavioral sessions and significant changes in both threshold and slope in 20/42 individual sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C36, C39, and C40 collectively demonstrate a robust and spatially-specific behavioral impairment. The data show significant increases in PDMI (p=0.02) in the attend-in condition but not in the attend-away condition, with control experiments ruling out thermal effects and visual distractions (C62, C63). The effect is replicated across multiple sessions with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: Low-frequency optogenetic stimulation increases low-frequency spike-count correlations among V4 neurons without significantly altering mean firing rates. The stimulation induces phase-locked neural activity and elevates correlations to levels comparable to those observed when attention is directed away from the receptive field.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C26, C29, and C32 are well-supported by physiological data in Figures 3A and 4. The authors successfully demonstrate increased correlations (p=0.045) while maintaining stable firing rates (p=0.49 pre-stimulus, p>0.1 stimulus period), achieving their goal of manipulating correlation structure independently of mean rate. Phase-locking analysis provides mechanistic insight into how the manipulation works.

results.result: High-frequency (20 Hz) optogenetic stimulation does not impair behavioral performance despite inducing high-frequency spike-count correlations and comparable phase-locking to low-frequency stimulation. Mean firing rates remain unchanged with high-frequency stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C41, and C42 establish the frequency-specificity of the behavioral effect, which is critical for the main conclusion. The data show no significant change in PDMI with high-frequency stimulation (Figure 2E) despite significant increases in high-frequency correlations (Figure 3B, p<0.05) and comparable phase-locking (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This dissociation strengthens the causal argument by ruling out non-specific effects of neural modulation.

results.result: Sessions with the strongest laser-induced perceptual impairment show corresponding reductions in neural discriminability (negative NDMI), with significant negative correlations between NDMI and PDMI (ρ=-0.29, p=0.05 for multi-dimensional analysis; ρ=-0.42, p=0.01 for pairwise analysis). This relationship is observed specifically on miss trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C52, C54, and C55 link the behavioral and neural effects through discriminability analysis. The negative correlation between NDMI and PDMI (Figure 5B) provides evidence that laser-induced correlations reduce neural discriminability in a manner that predicts behavioral impairment. The analysis appropriately focuses on miss trials and accounts for the positive signal correlations expected in V4's patchy organization. However, the correlation is modest and the lack of correlation with slope changes (C56) and hit trials (C57) suggests complexity in the relationship.

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrates that sub-threshold rhythmic stimulation can induce coherent activity in a conductance-based excitatory-inhibitory network at a desired frequency, and this induction is robust across a wide range of network and stimulation parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C58 and C59 are supported by the modeling results in Figure 6 and supplementary figures. The model successfully demonstrates the plausibility of the experimental manipulation, showing that sub-threshold stimulation can induce frequency-specific coherence. The robustness analysis across parameter space (Figure 6—figure supplements 1-2) strengthens this conclusion. However, the model is relatively simple and does not capture all aspects of cortical circuitry.

results.result: Control analyses rule out alternative explanations for the behavioral impairment: target stimulus onset shows no phase preference relative to laser stimulation, orientation tuning curves are not significantly altered by laser stimulation at either frequency, and there is no evidence of frequency-dependent adaptation that would reduce responses to visual stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C45, and C48 are supported by comprehensive control analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3-5. These controls address important alternative explanations: phase-dependent effects, tuning curve distortion, and adaptation. The two-way ANOVAs show no significant main effects of laser condition on tuning (p=0.37 for low-freq, p=0.82 for high-freq) or adaptation (p=0.52). These negative results strengthen the main conclusion by ruling out confounds.

results.result: The spatial specificity of the behavioral impairment and control experiments rule out phosphene effects, thermal effects, and visual distractions from the laser light as explanations for the observed behavioral changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by the spatial specificity of the effect (no impairment in attend-away condition) and direct control experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). The logic is sound: if a phosphene drew attention away, the attend-away condition would show impairment, which it does not. Stimulation at non-opsin sites and outside the brain produced no behavioral changes, ruling out thermal and visual distraction artifacts.

results.result: The artificial dura approach enables optogenetic manipulation in awake-behaving primates, with lenti-viral expression of C1V1 in excitatory neurons producing functionally similar orientation tuning among neurons within each injection site.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 describe the methodological approach, which is supported by Figure 1 and prior publications. The artificial dura provides optical access, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows similar orientation tuning within sites. However, the lack of histological verification of cell-type specificity in V4 (acknowledged in C64) is a limitation, though the authors provide reasonable justification based on prior work in V1 (C65) and other areas (C66).

results.result: While direct histological verification in V4 is unavailable, it is reasonable to assume strong bias toward pyramidal neurons based on prior work showing that lenti/CaMKII expressing C1V1/EYFP led to highly selective expression in excitatory neurons in macaque V1 (1.7% co-labeling with inhibitory markers) and perirhinal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 acknowledge a significant limitation: lack of direct histological verification of cell-type specificity in the current study. While the inference based on prior work in V1 and perirhinal cortex is reasonable, the assumption of similar selectivity in V4 remains unverified. This uncertainty affects interpretation of the mechanism, though it does not invalidate the main behavioral and correlational findings. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.

results.result: Behavioral performance on foil trials (where orientation change occurred at the uncued location) was impaired with slower reaction times, indicating that monkeys were using the spatial cue to deploy attention.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A showing reduced performance and slower reaction times for foil trials. This control is essential for validating that the task engaged spatial attention as intended. The result is straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: The study establishes the first causal link between correlated variability and perception, demonstrating the causal relevance of low-frequency correlated variability in perception and supporting the hypothesis that attention-dependent reductions in correlated variability enhance perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C69 represent the main conclusion of the study. This is supported by the convergence of behavioral impairment (C3-C4), increased low-frequency correlations (C3), frequency-specificity (C5), spatial specificity (C40), and correlation with neural discriminability (C54-C55). The causal claim is justified by the experimental manipulation, though the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations regarding the physiological realism of the induced correlations (C68).

results.result: Prior work has established that spatial attention reduces low-frequency correlated variability among V4 neurons, with this reduction estimated to account for approximately 80% of attention-mediated improvements in sensory processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C9-C12 accurately summarize prior literature on attention and correlations in V4, particularly work by Mitchell et al. (2009) and Cohen and Maunsell (2009). These claims provide appropriate context for the current study. The citations appear accurate and the characterization of prior findings is fair.

results.result: Prior theoretical and empirical work on the relationship between correlated variability and perception has yielded mixed conclusions, with estimates depending on assumptions about neural readout, and the causal role of correlated variability in perception remaining untested prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 provide a balanced review of the controversy in the field, citing both supportive (C15) and contradictory (C14, C16-C17) evidence regarding the role of correlations in perception. The identification of the gap in causal evidence (C18) appropriately motivates the current study. The characterization of prior work appears accurate and fair.

results.result: There was no significant correlation between neural discriminability modulation (NDMI) and changes in psychometric function slope, and NDMI calculated from hit trials showed no correlation with threshold or slope changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56 and C57 report negative results that are important for understanding the specificity of the neural-behavioral relationship. These findings suggest that the correlation between NDMI and behavioral impairment is specific to threshold changes and miss trials, which is consistent with the hypothesis but also indicates complexity in the relationship. The negative results are appropriately reported.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that the optogenetic stimulation protocol may induce correlations that are not physiologically realistic, but speculate that the induced correlations included information-limiting correlations. They propose that the timescale of low-frequency correlations is consistent with inter-saccadic intervals (200-300 ms), which may be a relevant timeframe for visual information gathering.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C70-C72 represent appropriate acknowledgment of limitations and speculation about mechanisms. The concern about physiological realism (C68) is valid, and the speculation about information-limiting correlations (C70) and inter-saccadic timescales (C71-C72) is reasonable but remains untested. These claims appropriately distinguish between what was demonstrated and what remains speculative.
